title: How LLMs Work
tagline: Large language models predict the next token — and from that single objective, language understanding emerges.

sections.content:
In late 2022, a chatbot answered a coding question, wrote a sonnet, and debugged a Python script in the same conversation — and the world took notice. Large Language Models (LLMs) are the technology behind today's AI assistants and coding tools. But what are they, actually? The honest one-sentence answer is: **a neural network trained to predict the next token in a sequence of text** — and then further trained, with human feedback and reinforcement learning, to be a useful assistant. The apparent reasoning, creativity, and knowledge emerge from doing that at extraordinary scale, on a large fraction of the text, code, and books available in digital form.

Understanding LLMs is no longer academic. If you write software today, you will call an LLM API, evaluate model responses, manage context windows, or debug a prompt that stopped working. The engineers who build reliable LLM-powered systems understand the mechanics: tokens, embeddings, the Transformer architecture, training dynamics, and inference behaviour. Without that foundation, you are flying blind.

This chapter builds that foundation systematically. We will walk through **six core concepts**: (1) tokenisation — how text becomes integers; (2) embeddings — how integers become geometry; (3) the Transformer — how context is processed via attention; (4) training — how weights are learned from trillions of tokens; (5) inference — how frozen weights generate new text; and (6) alignment and post-training — how raw prediction becomes a helpful assistant, and how reasoning models are trained. Along the way we will look at real code, work through the attention formula by hand, and examine the edge cases that trip up practitioners.

A brief orientation: LLMs have a **knowledge cutoff** (they do not know events after their training data), they can **hallucinate** (state false information confidently), and they are **stateless** between API calls (the illusion of memory is just a long context). These are not bugs to be fixed with better prompting — they are direct consequences of the architecture we are about to explore.

sections.title: An Extraordinarily Well-Read Autocomplete
sections.content:
Your phone's keyboard suggests the next word as you type. An LLM is conceptually the same mechanism — but trained on trillions of words of text and code rather than your personal messages, with billions of learned parameters instead of a simple frequency table, and looking at thousands to millions of prior tokens instead of the last two or three words.

The analogy also reveals the key limitation: autocomplete learns statistical patterns over text, and an LLM is, at bottom, also a learned model of text. At sufficient scale those patterns support behaviour that looks a lot like understanding — following novel instructions, writing working code, explaining why a recursive function overflows the stack — but the model can also produce fluent, confident text that is simply wrong, because "plausible continuation" and "true statement" are not the same objective. How much of this counts as genuine reasoning is an open research question; for engineering purposes, treat the output as a strong but fallible draft.

The critical architectural difference between phone autocomplete and LLMs is **attention**: autocomplete looks at a fixed short window of recent words. An LLM's self-attention mechanism looks at **every single token in the context simultaneously**, weighting each one's relevance. When completing 'The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of...', attention routes focus toward 'Eiffel Tower' even if hundreds of unrelated tokens separate the phrase from the blank — because the attention weights learned that those three tokens together predict 'Paris' with high probability. That global, parallel, learned relevance weighting is what makes LLMs qualitatively different from everything that came before.

sections.title: Tokenisation: How Text Becomes Numbers
sections.content:
Before any neural network can process text, the text must become numbers. **Tokens** are the atomic units that an LLM sees — neither characters nor words, but something in between.

The most common algorithm is **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)**, invented in 1994 for data compression and adapted for NLP in 2016. BPE starts from individual characters (or, in modern byte-level BPE, raw bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, stopping when the vocabulary reaches a target size. Vocabularies typically range from about 32,000 to over 200,000 tokens (Llama 3, for example, uses about 128,000). The result: very common words like 'the' or 'is' are a single token; rarer words like 'tokenisation' split into subwords like `['token', 'isation']`; completely unseen strings fall back to smaller pieces or individual bytes, so there is never an "unknown word". SentencePiece and WordPiece are related subword schemes used by other model families.

This matters practically for several reasons. First, **token count determines cost**: every API call bills by input and output tokens. Second, **token count determines speed**: each new token requires a full forward pass through the model. Third, **different languages tokenise differently**: English is ~0.75 words per token; many other languages — and especially non-Latin scripts — need noticeably more tokens for the same content, because they were a smaller share of the data the tokenizer was built from, so they cost more and fill the context faster.

A worked example: the string `'Hello, world!'` tokenises to `[9906, 11, 1917, 0]` — four tokens (`Hello`, `,`, ` world`, `!`) — in OpenAI's `cl100k_base` tokenizer; note the leading space is part of the ` world` token. A long rare word like `'antidisestablishmentarianism'` splits into several subword pieces, and `'1234567890'` into a few chunks, with the exact split depending on the tokenizer. Code and non-English text often need more tokens per character than English prose.

**Token IDs are just integers** — indices into the vocabulary table. The integer `9906` does not mean 'Hello'; it means 'row 9906 in our embedding matrix'. Meaning is not in the integer — it is in the embedding vector that integer indexes.

flowchart TD
    A["Raw string: unhappiness"] --> B["BPE split"]
    B --> C["un | happ | iness"]
    C --> D["Token IDs (illustrative): [348, 71, 2083]"]
    D --> E["Embedding lookup"]

sections.title: Embeddings: How Numbers Become Geometry
sections.content:
A token ID like `9906` is just a row number. To give it meaning, the model looks up a row in the **embedding matrix** — a learned table of shape `(vocab_size, d_model)`. For Llama 3 8B, with a vocabulary of about 128,000 tokens and a hidden dimension of 4,096, the embedding matrix holds about 525 million numbers — roughly 1 GB in 16-bit precision.

The resulting vector is a point in high-dimensional space. The remarkable property — not hard-coded, but **learned during training** — is that semantically similar tokens end up geometrically close. 'king', 'queen', 'monarch', 'ruler' cluster near each other. 'Paris', 'London', 'Tokyo' cluster near each other. The famous example from Word2Vec: `embedding('king') - embedding('man') + embedding('woman') ≈ embedding('queen')`. Arithmetic on vectors corresponds to semantic relationships.

But token embeddings alone have no positional information, and self-attention by itself treats its input as an unordered set. The word 'dog' has the same embedding whether it appears first or last in a sentence — and yet position matters enormously for meaning. The original Transformer added fixed sinusoidal **positional encodings** to each embedding; GPT-2 and GPT-3 learned an absolute position embedding per index; most current open models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and others) instead use **Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)**, which rotates the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to position so that attention scores depend on *relative* distance.

The combination — token embedding plus positional encoding — is the input to the first Transformer layer. After this point, the model works purely in this continuous vector space; it never sees characters or integers again until it produces its final output.

sections.title: The Transformer: Architecture of the Revolution
sections.content:
The Transformer was introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' by Vaswani et al. at Google. Before it, the dominant sequence models were RNNs (Recurrent Neural Networks) — networks that process tokens one at a time, maintaining a hidden state. RNNs had two fatal flaws: they could not parallelise (you must finish token 5 before processing token 6), and they struggled to retain information from very early in a long sequence (the **vanishing gradient problem**).

The Transformer abandoned recurrence entirely. It processes all tokens in parallel using **attention** — a mechanism that lets each token directly read from every other token in the context regardless of distance. This enables two things: massively parallel training on modern GPU hardware, and direct (one-step) access to any earlier position in the context window instead of information having to survive a long chain of recurrent updates.

A GPT-style (decoder-only) Transformer is a stack of **N identical blocks**. Each block contains two sub-layers:

**1. Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA)**: The core operation. Each token computes a query vector `Q`, a key vector `K`, and a value vector `V` via three learned weight matrices. The attention output is:

`Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q Kᵀ / sqrt(d_k)) V`

Intuitively: each token (via its query Q) scans all other tokens (via their keys K) to compute relevance scores. Softmax converts scores to weights that sum to 1. The output is a weighted sum of all tokens' value vectors. Multiple attention heads run in parallel — each head learns to look for different relationship types (syntactic, semantic, coreference, etc.). Heads' outputs are concatenated and projected back to `d_model`.

**Causal masking** makes the model autoregressive: position `i` may attend only to positions `0..i`. It is implemented by adding −∞ to the scores for future positions before the softmax, so their weights become exactly zero. The mask is used in training — where the model predicts every position of a sequence in parallel without peeking at the answer — and in the parallel prefill pass at inference. When generating, the newest token has no future tokens to hide, so each decode step simply attends to everything already in the KV-cache.

**2. Feed-Forward Network (FFN)**: After attention mixes information across tokens, the FFN processes each token's representation independently through an MLP with a non-linearity: classically `FFN(x) = W₂ · activation(W₁x + b₁) + b₂` with an inner dimension of 4× the model width. Most current LLMs use a gated variant, **SwiGLU**, with three weight matrices and an inner width around 2.7–3.5× (Llama 3 8B: 4,096 → 14,336). The FFN holds most of the parameters and is thought to store much of the model's factual "knowledge". **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** models replace this dense FFN with many expert FFNs plus a small router that sends each token to only a few of them (e.g. 2 of 64), so a model can have a very large *total* parameter count while each token only uses a small *active* fraction — more capacity for the same compute per token, at the cost of more memory to hold all the experts.

**Residual connections and normalisation** wrap both sub-layers. The original Transformer used post-norm, `x = LayerNorm(x + sublayer(x))`; virtually all modern LLMs use **pre-norm**, `x = x + sublayer(Norm(x))`, usually with RMSNorm, because it trains more stably at depth. The residual path lets gradients flow directly to early layers, and normalisation keeps activations in a stable range.

For scale, GPT-3 (2020) — whose architecture was published — has 96 layers, a model dimension of 12,288, 96 attention heads, and 175 billion parameters. Frontier labs no longer publish these details, and today's largest models are widely reported to be Mixture-of-Experts designs.

flowchart TD
    A["Token embeddings (+ RoPE inside attention)"]
    A --> N1["RMSNorm"]
    N1 --> B["Masked multi-head self-attention"]
    B --> C["Add residual"]
    C --> N2["RMSNorm"]
    N2 --> D["Feed-forward network (SwiGLU or MoE)"]

sections.caption: One modern (pre-norm) decoder block. Each sub-layer reads a normalised copy of the residual stream and adds its output back. After N blocks, a final projection maps hidden states to vocabulary-sized logits for the next-token distribution.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The attention computation: Q[0] matches K[0] (both [1,0]), giving the only non-zero score. After softmax, about 50% of token 0's output comes from V[0], with the rest split between the other two values. The causal-mask loop shows what a decoder actually computes: the first row can only attend to itself, and each later row sees one more token. The sqrt(dk) scaling is crucial — dot products of d-dimensional vectors grow roughly like √d, so without scaling the softmax saturates toward one-hot, and the gradients through all the non-maximal positions shrink toward zero.

sections.title: Multi-Head Attention: Why Multiple Heads?
sections.content:
A single attention head applies one set of Q, K, V projection matrices — learning one particular 'type' of relevance across the sequence. In practice, a sentence has many simultaneous relationship types: syntactic agreement ('cats' is plural, 'are' must be plural), semantic similarity ('Paris' relates to 'city'), coreference ('she' refers to 'Alice'), and more.

**Multi-head attention** runs `h` attention heads in parallel, each with its own learned Q, K, V projections of dimension `d_k = d_model / h`. The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected back to `d_model` via a final weight matrix `W_O`. The cost is the same as one head with dimension `d_model` (because `h × d_k = d_model`), but the model can simultaneously attend to different subspaces.

Analysis of trained models shows this is not just theoretical: different heads do specialise. In language models, some heads track syntactic structure, others handle long-range coreferences, others handle local collocations. The multi-head structure is a key reason why Transformers handle diverse linguistic phenomena better than any single attention pattern could.

For the numbers: Llama 3 8B uses `h=32` query heads with `d_model=4096`, so each head works in `d_k=128` dimensions — but only 8 key/value heads, shared by groups of four query heads (grouped-query attention, see below). GPT-3 used 96 heads with `d_model=12288`, also `d_k=128`; 64–128 dimensions per head is the common choice.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Input x (d_model)"] --> B["Head 1\nQ1,K1,V1"]
    A --> C["Head 2\nQ2,K2,V2"]
    A --> D["Head h\nQh,Kh,Vh"]
    B --> E["Concat"]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F["W_O projection"]
    F --> G["Output (d_model)"]
sections.caption: Multi-head attention: h parallel heads each with dimension d_k = d_model/h. Outputs are concatenated and reprojected, keeping the total dimensionality constant.

sections.title: Training: Learning from the Entire Internet
sections.content:
How do you teach a model to do all of this? Mostly through **next-token prediction** on an enormous corpus; everything else is fine-tuning on top. The training objective is deceptively simple:

Given tokens `t₁, t₂, ..., tₙ`, the model predicts `tₙ₊₁`. Loss = cross-entropy between predicted distribution and the true next token. Summed over billions of positions. Gradients computed via backpropagation. Weights updated via the AdamW optimiser. Repeat for weeks to months on thousands of GPUs.

**The scale of training** is staggering. GPT-3 was trained on about 300 billion tokens; Llama 3's 8B and 70B models were each trained on about 15 trillion tokens. A useful rule of thumb is that training costs about **6 × parameters × tokens** floating-point operations (2 for the forward pass, 4 for the backward pass) — for an 8B model on 15T tokens, roughly 7 × 10²³ FLOPs. Frontier training runs reportedly cost from tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in compute. This is done once per model version — the same weights then serve millions of users.

**Why does next-token prediction produce such capable models?** Because accurate prediction rewards modelling almost everything about the text: grammar (wrong grammar makes unlikely next tokens), facts (wrong facts make unlikely continuations), logic (wrong reasoning makes non sequitur continuations), and even emotional tone. The model that best predicts text is implicitly the model that best models the world that produced the text. This is the key intuition: **the training objective is a proxy for modelling the world that produced the text** — imperfectly, and only as far as the text reflects it.

**Pre-training vs. fine-tuning**: The process above is **pre-training** — training on raw internet text. The result is a **base model** that is good at predicting text but does not follow instructions, refuses nothing, and may produce harmful content. Fine-tuning adapts the base model for specific applications:

- **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**: Show the model examples of (instruction, ideal response) pairs. Train with the same next-token loss but only on the response portion. This teaches instruction following and the chat format.
- **RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)**: Human raters compare pairs of model outputs. A separate **reward model** is trained to predict which response people prefer, and the LLM is then optimised with reinforcement learning (classically PPO) to maximise that reward, with a penalty for drifting too far from the SFT model. Variants replace some human labels with AI feedback guided by written principles (RLAIF / Constitutional AI).
- **DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation)** and related methods: optimise directly on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss, without training a separate reward model or running an RL loop. Cheaper and more stable, and widely used — often alongside RL rather than instead of it.
- **Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards**: for maths, coding, and other checkable tasks, the model is rewarded when its final answer passes a test or matches a known result. Large-scale RL of this kind is how **reasoning models** are trained (see below).

**Emergent capabilities** are abilities that appear at scale without explicit training. Below a certain parameter count, models cannot reliably do chain-of-thought reasoning or multi-step arithmetic. Above it, the capability appears, seemingly spontaneously. This has led to debate about whether capability jumps are truly emergent or just artefacts of how we measure performance.

flowchart TD

(raw internet text, trillions of tokens)"] --> B["Base Model
(predicts next token)"] 
    B --> C["Supervised Fine-Tuning

sections.title: Reasoning Models, Mixture-of-Experts, and Tool Use
sections.content:
Two architectural and training shifts define current models, and both change how you use them.

**Reasoning models and test-time compute.** Instead of answering immediately, a reasoning model is trained (largely with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks) to generate a long internal chain of thought — exploring approaches, checking intermediate results, and backtracking — before producing its final answer. Accuracy on hard maths, coding, and multi-step problems keeps improving as the model is allowed to "think" for more tokens, so **inference-time compute** becomes a second scaling axis alongside model size and training data. The costs are latency and tokens: a hard question may consume thousands of reasoning tokens that you pay for even if you never see them, so many APIs expose a knob for reasoning effort or a thinking-token budget.

**Mixture-of-Experts.** Many large models now route each token through only a few of many expert feed-forward networks. Quote MoE sizes as "total / active" parameters: total parameters determine the memory you need to host the model, while active parameters per token determine the compute (and roughly the speed) of each step. This is why an MoE model can be both very large and relatively fast.

**Tools and agents.** Post-training also teaches models to emit structured tool calls (search, code execution, APIs) that the application executes and feeds back into the context. An "agent" is simply this loop — model proposes an action, the harness runs it, the result is appended, repeat — so its reliability depends as much on the tools, permissions, and checks around the model as on the model itself.

sections.title: Inference: Generating Text Token by Token
sections.content:
Once training is complete, the model's weights are **frozen**. Inference is how the frozen model generates new text.

When you send a message to an LLM API, the following happens:

1. **Tokenise the prompt**: Your text is converted to a sequence of token IDs.
2. **Prefill (parallel forward pass)**: All prompt tokens are processed simultaneously in a single forward pass through all N Transformer layers. This produces the KV tensors for every prompt token and the logits for the last position. This step is compute-bound.
3. **Decode (autoregressive generation)**: Using the logits from the last position, sample or select the next token. Append it to the sequence. Run another forward pass — but now the KV-cache means you only compute the new token's Q, K, V and attend to cached K, V from all previous tokens. This step is memory-bandwidth-bound.
4. **Repeat** until `<EOS>` (end-of-sequence) token or max length.

**The KV-cache** is the critical optimisation that makes inference tractable. Without it, generating token `n` would mean recomputing the keys and values of all `n−1` previous tokens at every layer, so producing a long answer would cost O(n²) projection work on top of attention. With the KV-cache, each step computes K and V only for the new token, appends them, and attends over the cached entries — O(n) memory reads per step. The trade-off is memory: per token, the cache stores `2 (K and V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes`. For Llama 3 8B in 16-bit precision that is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = **128 KiB per token**, or about **16 GiB for a single 128K-token context** — more than the model's own weights. This is why KV-cache size, not compute, usually limits how many requests a GPU can serve at once, and why grouped-query attention, cache quantisation, and paged cache management (vLLM's PagedAttention) matter so much.

**Sampling strategies** control how a token is chosen from the logit distribution:
- **Greedy**: always pick the highest-probability token. Deterministic but often repetitive.
- **Temperature sampling**: divide logits by temperature `T` before softmax. `T < 1` sharpens the distribution (more deterministic); `T > 1` flattens it (more random). `T = 0` approaches greedy.
- **Top-k sampling**: restrict sampling to the k highest-probability tokens. Cuts off the long tail of low-probability choices.
- **Top-p (nucleus) sampling**: sample from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds `p`. Adapts the number of candidates to the distribution's shape.
- **Beam search**: maintain the top-B sequences in parallel, selecting the globally highest-probability full sequence. Used in translation; rarely in chat models (too repetitive).
- **Speculative decoding**: a small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model verifies them in one parallel pass — identical output distribution, often 2–3× faster decoding.

Most production LLM APIs default to some combination of temperature + top-p sampling. The exact combination dramatically affects output quality and style.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Temperature controls the sharpness of the probability distribution before sampling. At T=0 the highest-probability token is always chosen (greedy). As T increases, lower-probability tokens become more likely, introducing variety. Top-p (nucleus) sampling adapts the candidate set dynamically — it keeps the smallest set of tokens covering p of the probability mass, which means more candidates when the model is uncertain and fewer when it is confident (here just two). The context check reserves room for the output because prompt and completion share the same window; the limits are placeholders, since real models' windows change with every release.

sections.title: The Context Window: Working Memory with a Hard Limit
sections.content:
The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single forward pass. Everything inside the context window is directly accessible — attention can connect any two positions (though, as the "lost in the middle" results show, not always equally well). Everything outside is completely invisible.

Context lengths have grown dramatically: GPT-2 (2019) had 1,024 tokens; by 2025–26, windows of hundreds of thousands of tokens were standard and some models accepted a million or more. Each jump required engineering effort because naive attention scales as `O(n²)` in compute — doubling context length quadruples the attention cost — and the KV-cache grows linearly with context.

Solutions for long contexts include:
- **FlashAttention**: A hardware-aware algorithm that computes attention in tiles held in fast on-chip SRAM, never writing the full `n×n` score matrix to the GPU's main memory (HBM). Same mathematical output, attention memory that grows linearly instead of quadratically, and much faster in practice because it is memory-bandwidth-bound work done more efficiently.
- **Sliding window attention**: Each token attends only to a local window of recent positions. Used in Longformer, Mistral 7B, and (interleaved with global layers) several recent models. It caps the per-token cost at the expense of not having full global attention in those layers.
- **Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)**: Groups of query heads share one key/value head (Multi-Query Attention is the extreme case: one K/V head for all). This shrinks the KV-cache by the group factor — 4× for Llama 3 8B — with little quality loss.
- **RoPE scaling for long context**: RoPE does *not* automatically generalise far beyond the lengths seen in training; long-context models extend it with position interpolation or frequency-scaling schemes (NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) plus additional training on long documents.

From an application perspective, the context window is **working memory**. The model cannot remember previous conversations that have scrolled out of the window or were never sent. This is why chat applications maintain a conversation history buffer, trim it when it grows too large, and sometimes use summarisation to compress older turns. **Prompt caching**, offered by the major LLM APIs, lets the server reuse the computed KV-cache for an identical prompt prefix (a long system prompt, a document, tool definitions), cutting latency and cost for requests that share it — which is why stable content should go first in the prompt and variable content last.

sections.title: Hallucination, Uncertainty, and Knowledge Cutoffs
sections.content:
Three limitations of LLMs are direct consequences of the architecture, not implementation flaws:

**Hallucination**: LLMs generate a probable continuation of a sequence. When the answer is not well represented in the training data, the model still generates text — plausible-sounding text that may be factually wrong. Nothing in the pre-training objective rewards saying "I don't know"; post-training can teach models to abstain or express uncertainty, which reduces hallucination but does not eliminate it. Hallucination is worst for specific low-frequency facts (exact numbers, dates, citations, API signatures) and rarer for well-documented topics.

**Knowledge cutoff**: Training data has a cutoff date, and the model knows little or nothing about later events (models are often unsure of their own cutoff, too). Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and tool use — web search, database queries — are the standard solutions: fetch up-to-date documents at inference time, inject them into the context window, and instruct the model to answer from those sources rather than from its parametric memory.

**Weak self-reported uncertainty**: A model that writes "I am 95% confident" is generating text, not reading out a calibrated internal probability. Token-level probabilities are often reasonably calibrated for base models, but they measure confidence in the *next token*, not in the *claim*, and preference tuning tends to make models sound more confident than they are. For high-stakes uses, measure accuracy on your own evaluation set instead of trusting stated confidence, and add verification (citations you can check, tests, human review).

These are properties of the training objective, not bugs that a patch will remove — they can be reduced, not eliminated. Understanding them lets you design around them: use RAG for facts, use retrieval for recency, use structured output validation to catch hallucinated formats, and use human review for high-stakes claims.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["User Query"] --> B["Embed query"]
    B --> C["Vector Search\n(cosine similarity)"]
    C --> D["Retrieved Chunks\n(top-k documents)"]
    D --> E["Augmented Prompt\n= query + retrieved docs"]
    E --> F["LLM generates\nanswer from context"]
    F --> G["Response"]
sections.caption: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): retrieved document chunks are inserted into the context window, allowing the model to ground its answer in current, specific facts rather than parametric memory.

sections.title: Model Size, Scaling Laws, and Parameter Counts
sections.content:
LLM parameter counts are frequently cited but rarely explained. **Parameters** are the learned weights — the Q, K, V, and output projection matrices, the FFN weights, the embedding matrix, and the output head. For a classic decoder-only Transformer, the dominant costs are:

- Embedding matrix: `vocab_size × d_model` (e.g. 128,000 × 4,096 ≈ 524M for Llama 3 8B), plus an output head of the same size unless the two are weight-tied
- Per Transformer block: `4 × d_model²` (attention) + `8 × d_model²` (FFN with 4× expansion) ≈ `12 × d_model²`
- For 32 layers: `32 × 12 × 4096² ≈ 6.4B` parameters
- Plus embedding and output head ≈ 7.5B — close to Llama 3 8B's real 8.0B (its wider SwiGLU FFN adds parameters, while grouped-query attention removes some)

The **Chinchilla scaling laws** (Hoffmann et al. 2022, DeepMind) established a crucial empirical finding: for a fixed *training* compute budget, you get a better model by training a **smaller model on more tokens** than a larger model on fewer — roughly 20 tokens per parameter is compute-optimal. In practice, labs now train far past that point because the resulting model is cheaper to *serve*: Llama 3 8B saw about 15 trillion tokens, roughly 1,900 tokens per parameter — nearly 100× the Chinchilla ratio — and kept improving.

The practical implication: model size alone does not determine capability. A well-trained small model can outperform a poorly-trained large model. When evaluating models, look at benchmark results on your task type, not just parameter counts.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The parameter estimate shows where the numbers come from: for Llama 3 8B the embedding and output matrices together are about a billion parameters, and each Transformer block adds roughly 200M. Weight tying matters at small scale — GPT-2 reuses its embedding matrix as the output head, which is why its estimate lands near the real 124M. The Chinchilla calculation shows how far modern models deliberately overtrain: a smaller model trained on far more tokens costs more to train but less to run, and inference cost dominates for widely used models. The 6·N·D rule gives a quick estimate of training compute.

sections.content: **A brief history:** The Transformer was published in June 2017 ('Attention Is All You Need', Vaswani et al.). BERT (2018, Google) showed bidirectional Transformers excel at understanding tasks; GPT-1 (2018, OpenAI) showed decoder-only Transformers work for generation. GPT-2 (2019) was released in stages over misuse concerns — 1.5B parameters seemed enormous at the time. GPT-3 (2020, 175B parameters) demonstrated few-shot learning from prompts alone. InstructGPT (2022) popularised RLHF for instruction following, and ChatGPT (November 2022) brought it to the public, reaching a reported 100 million users in about two months. 2023–24 brought multimodal models, open-weight model families, and context windows growing from thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens; 2024–25 brought reasoning models trained with large-scale reinforcement learning and widespread Mixture-of-Experts designs. The field went from research curiosity to mainstream infrastructure in about five years.

**Common misconceptions to clear up before interviews or production work:**

**'LLMs know the answer and are hiding it.'** No — the model generates the most probable continuation. There is no hidden 'real answer' being suppressed. If it gives a wrong answer confidently, it means wrong-but-plausible text had high probability given training data.

**'Temperature 0 is deterministic.'** Almost: `temperature=0` means greedy decoding, but outputs can still vary between identical calls. GPU floating-point arithmetic is not associative, so results depend on how requests are batched together and which kernels run; mixture-of-experts routing can amplify tiny differences. Never rely on bit-for-bit reproducibility unless the provider explicitly guarantees it.

**'More context is always better.'** Performance on tasks within the context window can degrade in very long contexts — the so-called 'lost in the middle' phenomenon where models attend poorly to content in the middle of very long inputs. For retrieval tasks, smaller well-curated context can outperform massive raw context.

**'A bigger model is always better.'** Training data quality and quantity, post-training, and inference-time reasoning matter as much as raw size. A well-trained small model can beat a much larger, older one on specific tasks — and costs far less to run. Always benchmark on your actual use case.

**'LLMs are looking things up.'** Base LLMs have no access to external tools or databases during inference — knowledge is baked into weights at training time. When you see a model 'search the web', that is an **external tool call** added by the application layer, not native model capability.

items: **Tokens** are subword text units produced by BPE tokenisation (~0.75 English words per token). Token count determines API cost, generation speed, and whether content fits in the context window. Token efficiency varies significantly across languages.

**Embeddings** map token IDs to dense vectors in a high-dimensional space where semantic similarity is encoded as geometric proximity. Positional encodings are added to give the model knowledge of token order, since self-attention is inherently position-agnostic.

**Self-attention** — `softmax(QKᵀ/sqrt(dk))V` — lets each token attend to every earlier token at once (a causal mask hides future positions). Multiple parallel heads specialise in different relationship types. The `sqrt(dk)` scaling prevents softmax saturation and gradient vanishing.

**Training** runs next-token prediction on trillions of tokens using cross-entropy loss and AdamW (compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens). This single objective implicitly requires the model to learn grammar, facts, reasoning, and world knowledge. Post-training — SFT, preference tuning (RLHF/DPO), and RL with verifiable rewards — then makes the base model useful, safe, and (for reasoning models) able to think step by step before answering.

**Inference** tokenises the prompt, runs a parallel prefill forward pass, then generates tokens autoregressively one at a time. The KV-cache avoids recomputing previous tokens' keys and values, but costs memory per token (128 KiB/token for Llama 3 8B in 16-bit), which is what limits concurrency and long contexts. Temperature and top-p sampling control output randomness.

**Hallucination and knowledge cutoffs** are fundamental architectural properties, not bugs. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is the standard mitigation: retrieve relevant, current documents and inject them into the context for the model to reason over.

**Scaling laws** (Chinchilla) show that compute budget is best spent on a smaller model trained on more tokens. Model size alone does not predict capability — training data quality, fine-tuning, and alignment all matter substantially.

**Modern variations**: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a few expert FFNs per token (quote "total / active" parameters); reasoning models spend extra inference-time tokens thinking before answering, trading latency and cost for accuracy on hard problems.

quiz.question: What is the primary training objective of a GPT-style large language model?
options: Classifying whether a sentence is grammatically correct
Translating text between different natural languages
Predicting the next token given all previous tokens in the sequence
Ranking documents by relevance to a query
quiz.explanation: GPT-style models are trained with a causal language modelling objective: given all previous tokens in a sequence, predict the next token. Cross-entropy loss penalises wrong predictions and gradients flow back to update weights. This single objective applied at enormous scale causes broad language understanding to emerge as a side-effect of learning to predict text accurately.

quiz.question: What is Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) and why is it used for tokenisation?
options: A tokenisation method that iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent character pairs to build a subword vocabulary
A compression algorithm that encodes each byte as a pair of bits
A technique that maps each word to exactly one token regardless of frequency
A way to convert text into floating-point vectors for the embedding layer
quiz.explanation: BPE starts from individual characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequently adjacent pair into a new vocabulary entry, until the target vocabulary size is reached. This produces a vocabulary where common words are single tokens and rare words decompose into known subword pieces, balancing vocabulary size against coverage of any input text without out-of-vocabulary errors.

quiz.question: In the attention formula `softmax(QKᵀ / sqrt(dk)) V`, what is the purpose of dividing by `sqrt(dk)`?
options: To normalise the attention weights so they sum to 1 across all heads
To convert raw logits into probability scores over the vocabulary
To apply positional information to the attention computation
To prevent dot products from growing large with high-dimensional keys, which would push softmax into saturation and cause vanishing gradients
quiz.explanation: For large dk, dot products of random Q and K vectors have a standard deviation that grows like sqrt(dk). Without scaling, large dot products push softmax toward a near-one-hot distribution, where essentially all weight collapses onto one token. This means gradients through all other attention positions vanish nearly to zero, severely hampering training. Dividing by sqrt(dk) keeps dot products in a stable range where softmax gradients remain healthy across all positions.

quiz.question: What does the KV-cache do during LLM inference, and why is it important?
options: It stores the vocabulary embeddings in fast memory to speed up tokenisation
It caches Key and Value matrices from previously processed tokens so they do not need to be recomputed on each new generation step
It is a database of common knowledge injected into the model at startup
It stores conversation history between separate API calls to maintain state
quiz.explanation: During autoregressive generation, each new token requires attention over all previous tokens. Without caching, all K and V matrices would be recomputed from scratch at every step — O(n²) work per new token. The KV-cache saves the K and V tensors from all previous positions in GPU memory. Each new decode step only computes the new token's K and V, then reads from the cache for all others. This is what makes generation fast enough to be practical.

quiz.question: What is the 'context window' of an LLM, and what happens to content that exceeds it?
options: The maximum number of tokens the model can process in one forward pass; content beyond it is completely invisible to the model
A sliding window that stores the most recent 10 conversation turns between API calls
The number of attention heads multiplied by the head dimension
The temperature range applied during sampling to control output randomness
quiz.explanation: The context window is the hard upper bound on tokens per inference call. The model's attention mechanism can connect any two positions within this window — but positions outside it do not exist from the model's perspective. Exceeding the limit requires truncating context, summarising older content, or using RAG to retrieve only the most relevant chunks. Window sizes vary widely between models and keep growing — from a few thousand tokens to a million or more — and the prompt and the generated output share the same window.

quiz.question: What is the difference between pre-training and RLHF fine-tuning in the LLM pipeline?
options: Pre-training uses attention; RLHF does not use attention
RLHF happens before pre-training to initialise the model's weights
Pre-training trains weights on next-token prediction over massive text corpora; RLHF fine-tunes the model using human preference rankings to make it helpful, honest, and harmless
Pre-training is done on GPU; RLHF is done on CPU
quiz.explanation: Pre-training learns weights from scratch by predicting the next token across trillions of tokens of raw internet text — this is the dominant compute cost. The result is a base model that is good at predicting text but does not follow instructions or have safety properties. RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) then fine-tunes the base model: human raters rank model outputs, a reward model learns to predict these rankings, and the LLM is updated with reinforcement learning (classically PPO) to maximise reward-model scores, producing an aligned assistant. DPO is a popular alternative that learns from the preference pairs directly, without a separate reward model.

quiz.question: What is 'hallucination' in the context of LLMs, and why does it occur?
options: A visual glitch caused by running the model at high temperature settings
When the model refuses to answer a question due to safety filters
A deliberate feature that allows the model to generate creative fictional content
When the model generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information because it produces the most probable token sequence regardless of factual grounding
quiz.explanation: LLMs generate the most statistically probable continuation of a token sequence. When the correct answer is not well-represented in training data, the model still produces text — it generates something that looks superficially like a plausible answer. There is no internal fact-checker or mechanism to signal 'I don't know this' and refuse. Hallucination is worst for specific low-frequency facts (obscure statistics, names, citations) and is mitigated by RAG, which grounds the model's response in retrieved documents.

quiz.question: What does temperature control in LLM sampling, and what does temperature=0 produce?
options: It controls the context window size; temperature=0 uses no context
It scales logits before softmax, controlling distribution sharpness; temperature=0 produces greedy decoding, always selecting the highest-probability token
It sets the learning rate during fine-tuning; temperature=0 freezes weights
It controls the number of transformer layers activated; temperature=0 uses only the first layer
quiz.explanation: Temperature is a scalar applied to logits before the softmax: logits are divided by T. Low T (< 1) sharpens the distribution toward the highest-probability token, making output more deterministic and factual but also more repetitive. High T (> 1) flattens the distribution, increasing output variety and creativity. At T→0, the softmax approaches a one-hot distribution on the argmax — this is greedy decoding, always picking the single most likely token.

quiz.question: What are Chinchilla scaling laws, and what do they imply about how to train LLMs?
options: Laws derived from chinchilla fur patterns showing that model weights should be sparsified like animal fur
Rules governing how model size must scale with context window length
Empirical findings that for a fixed compute budget, training a smaller model on proportionally more tokens (roughly 20 tokens per parameter) outperforms training a larger model on fewer tokens
Guidelines requiring that all LLMs must be evaluated on a standard chinchilla benchmark dataset
quiz.explanation: The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., DeepMind 2022) showed that previous large models like GPT-3 were significantly undertrained. With a fixed training-compute budget, the optimum is roughly 20 tokens per parameter: a 7B model should see about 140B tokens. GPT-3 (175B parameters, 300B tokens — under 2 tokens per parameter) was heavily undertrained by this measure. Modern models deliberately overtrain instead — Llama 3 8B saw ~15 trillion tokens — because a smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve.

quiz.question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and what problem does it solve?
options: An inference-time technique that retrieves relevant documents and injects them into the prompt, letting the model answer questions using current or private information not in its training weights
A training technique that retrieves similar training examples to augment loss computation
A method to increase the effective context window by compressing the KV-cache using retrieval
A hardware technique that retrieves model weights from secondary storage to reduce GPU memory usage
quiz.explanation: LLMs have a knowledge cutoff and cannot access information not in their training data. RAG addresses this: at inference time, the user query is embedded into a vector, similar document chunks are retrieved from a vector database (cosine similarity search), and those chunks are inserted into the prompt context. The model then generates its answer by reasoning over the retrieved documents rather than purely from parametric memory. This makes LLMs useful for private knowledge bases, up-to-date information, and reducing hallucination on factual questions.
